lesson.title: What Actually Runs Your Python Code
lesson.summary: The Python interpreter is the program that turns Python source code into an intermediate bytecode form and then executes that bytecode step by step, and it is the reason Python code can run at all.
lesson.body:
When you write Python code, you are writing text in a file or typing it directly at a prompt, but text by itself does nothing. Something has to read that text and actually carry out the instructions it describes. That something is the Python interpreter, a program whose entire job is to take Python source code and make the computer do what it says. The standard, most widely used implementation of the Python interpreter is called CPython, and it is itself written in the C programming language. Other implementations exist, such as PyPy, which is built for speed, but when most people type python at a terminal, they are running CPython.

The interpreter's work happens in two main stages, which connects directly back to the idea of compiled versus interpreted languages from the previous chapter. First, the interpreter reads your Python source code and translates it into an intermediate form called bytecode, a set of simpler, lower-level instructions that are still not the same as raw machine code but are much closer to something a program can execute quickly. This first stage resembles compilation. Second, a part of the interpreter called the Python Virtual Machine reads that bytecode and executes it, one instruction at a time. This second stage resembles interpretation. Python sometimes even saves this compiled bytecode to disk, in a hidden folder named __pycache__, so that if you run the same unchanged file again, the interpreter can skip re-translating it.

Tracing through a small example makes this concrete. Suppose a file named hello.py contains:

print("Start")
x = 2 + 3
print(x)

When you run python hello.py, the interpreter first reads the whole file and translates each line into bytecode. Roughly speaking, the first line becomes an instruction to load the text Start and call the print function on it. The second line becomes instructions to load the values 2 and 3, add them together, and store the result under the name x. The third line becomes an instruction to look up whatever x currently refers to and call print on it. Once translation is done, the Python Virtual Machine executes these bytecode instructions in order, from top to bottom: it prints Start, computes 2 + 3 to get 5 and stores that under x, then looks up x and prints 5.

This distinction matters because it explains behavior you will notice once you start running real programs. Because the interpreter processes your file from top to bottom, an error later in a file will not stop earlier lines from running first, and a mistake on a line that never actually executes, such as inside a branch that is never taken, may not be discovered at all until that exact line is reached. Understanding that the interpreter is doing real, sequential work each time you run a file also sets up the next two chapters, where you will see the two main ways people actually use this interpreter: typing commands one at a time, and running a saved script file all at once.
